title: Book II: Old And Young — Chapter XXI
paragraphs:
“Hire facounde eke full womanly and plain,
No contrefeted termes had she
To semen wise.”
—CHAUCER.

That was how Dorothea came to be sobbing once she knew she was alone. Soon a knock roused her. She hurriedly dried her eyes before calling, “Come in.” Tantripp brought a visiting card. A gentleman was waiting in the entrance hall. The traveling attendant had told him that only Mrs. Casaubon was at home, but he said he was related to Mr. Casaubon. Would she receive him?

“Yes,” Dorothea said immediately. “Show him into the sitting room.” Her strongest memories of young Ladislaw were of learning, when she saw him at Lowick, how generous Mr. Casaubon had been to him, and of taking an interest in his uncertainty about a career. She welcomed anything that offered a chance to put sympathy into action. At this moment the visit seemed to have come to shake her out of self-absorbed dissatisfaction, remind her of her husband’s goodness, and make her feel her new right to help him in every act of kindness. She waited a minute or two. When she entered the next room, just enough traces of crying remained to make her open face seem younger and more appealing than usual. She greeted Ladislaw with that exquisite smile of goodwill untouched by vanity and held out her hand. He was several years older, but at that moment looked much younger. His clear complexion flushed suddenly, and he spoke with a shyness entirely unlike his easy indifference with his male companion. Dorothea grew calmer still, wondering and wanting to put him at ease.

“I didn’t know you and Mr. Casaubon were in Rome until I saw you this morning in the Vatican Museum,” he said. “I recognized you at once, but—I mean, I assumed the post office would have Mr. Casaubon’s address, and I wanted to pay my respects to you both as soon as possible.”

“Please sit down. He isn’t here just now, but I’m sure he’ll be pleased to hear about you,” said Dorothea. Without thinking, she seated herself between the fire and the light from the tall window, indicating a chair opposite with the calm kindness of an older married woman. The traces of girlish sorrow in her face stood out all the more. “Mr. Casaubon is very busy. But you’ll leave your address, won’t you? Then he can write to you.”

“You’re very kind,” said Ladislaw, beginning to forget his shyness in his interest in the signs of tears that had changed her face. “My address is on the card. But if I may, I’ll call again tomorrow when Mr. Casaubon is likely to be at home.”

“He reads in the Vatican Library every day, so you’re unlikely to see him without an appointment. Especially now. We’re about to leave Rome, and he’s very busy. Usually he’s away almost from breakfast until dinner. But I’m sure he’ll want you to dine with us.”

Will Ladislaw was speechless for a moment. He had never liked Mr. Casaubon, and without his sense of obligation would have laughed at him as a bat living in the darkness of learning. But to think that this dried-up pedant, this manufacturer of little explanations about as valuable as the stock of fake antiquities in a dealer’s back room, had first persuaded this adorable young creature to marry him and then spent his honeymoon away from her, fumbling after his moldy trifles—Will tended to exaggerate—filled him with a kind of comic disgust. He was torn between laughing aloud and bursting into contemptuous abuse, both equally inappropriate.
For an instant he felt the struggle twisting his expressive face oddly. With an effort, he turned it into nothing more offensive than a cheerful smile.

Dorothea wondered, but the smile was irresistible and shone back from her own face. Unless you were already angry with him, Will Ladislaw’s smile was delightful. It was a rush of inward light illuminating his clear skin as well as his eyes, playing over every line and curve as though an Ariel had touched them with fresh charm and banished every trace of moodiness forever. Its reflection inevitably carried a little laughter too, even beneath Dorothea’s still-damp dark lashes, as she asked, “Something amuses you?”
“Yes,” said Will, quick to find an explanation. “I’m remembering the figure I cut when we first met and you demolished my poor sketch with your criticism.”
“My criticism?” Dorothea asked, more puzzled than ever. “Surely not. I always feel especially ignorant about painting.”

“I suspected you knew so much that you could choose exactly the most cutting thing to say. You said—I don’t suppose you remember it as I do—that you couldn’t see any connection between my sketch and nature. At least, that was the implication.” Will could now laugh as well as smile.

“That truly was ignorance,” said Dorothea, admiring his good humor. “I must have said it because I could never find beauty in the pictures my uncle told me all the experts admired. I’ve been going about Rome in just the same ignorance. There are relatively few paintings I can really enjoy. When I first enter a room covered in frescoes or rare pictures, I feel something like awe, like a child at a great ceremony with splendid robes and processions. I feel in the presence of a life higher than my own. But as soon as I examine the pictures separately, the life leaves them, or becomes something violent and unfamiliar. It must be my own dullness. I’m seeing so much at once and understanding less than half. That always makes one feel stupid. It’s painful to be told something is very fine and be unable to feel its beauty—rather like being blind while people talk about the sky.”

“Oh, a great deal of appreciation for art has to be learned,” said Will. He could no longer doubt her confession’s sincerity. “Art is an old language with many artificial, affected styles. Sometimes the chief pleasure in knowing them is simply the feeling that one knows. I enjoy all kinds of art here enormously. But if I took that enjoyment apart, I imagine I’d find many different strands. Dabbling in paint yourself and understanding something of the process makes a difference.”
“Perhaps you intend to become a painter?” Dorothea asked, her interest taking a new direction. “To make it your profession? Mr. Casaubon will be glad to hear you’ve chosen a career.”

“No, certainly not,” said Will rather coldly. “I’ve definitely decided against it. The life is too one-sided. I’ve seen a great deal of the German artists here; I traveled from Frankfurt with one of them. Some are splendid, even brilliant fellows. But I wouldn’t want to acquire their habit of seeing the whole world from the studio.”

“I can understand that,” said Dorothea warmly. “Here in Rome there seem to be so many things the world needs more than pictures. Still, if you have a genius for painting, shouldn’t you let it guide you? Perhaps you could make better things than these, or different ones, so there wouldn’t be so many almost identical pictures in one place.”

Her sincerity was unmistakable, and it drew Will into frankness. “It takes a very rare genius to change things that way. I’m afraid mine wouldn’t even let me do well what others have already done—at least, not well enough to justify it. And I could never succeed through sheer drudgery. If something doesn’t come easily, I never master it.”
“I’ve heard Mr. Casaubon say he regrets your lack of patience,” Dorothea said gently. She was rather shocked by this way of treating all life as a holiday.
“Yes, I know his opinion. We disagree.”
The faint streak of contempt in this quick answer offended Dorothea. The morning’s distress made her especially sensitive about her husband.
“You certainly differ,” she said rather proudly. “I wasn’t comparing you. Mr. Casaubon’s capacity for sustained, devoted work is uncommon.”

Will saw he had offended her, but that only sharpened his newly stirred, underlying dislike of Mr. Casaubon. Dorothea’s worship of her husband was intolerable. No man enjoys that weakness in a woman except the husband she worships. We mortals are easily tempted to pinch the life out of a neighbor’s buzzing glory and persuade ourselves such killing is no murder.

“Uncommon indeed,” he answered at once. “Which makes it a pity to waste it, as so much English scholarship is wasted, through ignorance of what the rest of the world is doing. Mr. Casaubon could save himself a great deal of trouble if he read German.”
“I don’t understand,” said Dorothea, startled and anxious.

“I only mean,” Will said casually, “that the Germans lead the way in historical research. They laugh at results obtained by wandering through woods with a pocket compass when they’ve already built good roads. When I was with Mr. Casaubon, I saw how he shut his ears to them. He would scarcely read even a Latin treatise by a German. I was very sorry about it.”

Will was thinking only of delivering a sharp pinch to destroy that much-praised industry. He could not imagine how his words would wound Dorothea. Young Mr. Ladislaw was far from deeply read in German authors himself. But it takes very little achievement to pity another man’s deficiencies.

Poor Dorothea felt such pain at the thought that her husband’s life’s work might be worthless that she had no energy left to consider whether this young relative, so indebted to him, should have kept his observation to himself. She said nothing, only looked at her hands, absorbed by the thought’s pitiable sadness.

After delivering his crushing pinch, however, Will felt ashamed. He took her silence to mean he had offended her further, and his conscience also troubled him over plucking the tail feathers from a benefactor.

“I was particularly sorry,” he resumed, following the usual path from disparagement to insincere praise, “because of my gratitude and respect for my cousin. It would matter less in someone whose abilities and character were less distinguished.”

Dorothea looked up, her eyes brighter than usual with stirred feeling, and said in her saddest, musical tone, “How I wish I’d learned German at Lausanne! There were so many German teachers. But now I can’t help at all.”

These last words cast a new, though still mysterious, light for Will. When he first saw her, he had answered the question of how she came to accept Mr. Casaubon by deciding she must be disagreeable despite her looks. That quick, easy explanation would no longer do. Whatever else she was, she was not disagreeable. She was not coldly clever or slyly satirical, but adorably direct and full of feeling. She was an angel deceived. It would be a unique delight to wait and watch for the musical fragments in which her heart and soul revealed themselves so plainly and innocently. Once again he thought of an Aeolian harp.

She must have invented some unusual romance for herself in marrying him. If Mr. Casaubon had been a dragon who simply seized her in his claws and carried her to his cave without legal formalities, rescuing her and falling at her feet would have been an unavoidable act of heroism. But he was harder to manage than a dragon. He was a benefactor with the whole of society behind him. At that moment he entered the room in all the faultless correctness of his manner. Dorothea’s face was alive with newly awakened alarm and regret, while Will’s was animated by his admiring guesses about her feelings.

Mr. Casaubon’s surprise contained no pleasure, but he maintained his customary polite greeting as Will stood and explained his visit. He was less happy than usual, which may have made him seem still dimmer and more faded. Otherwise the contrast with his young cousin could easily have produced that effect. Will’s first impression was one of sunny brightness, adding to the elusiveness of his shifting expression. Surely his very features changed shape: his jaw looked large one moment and small the next, and the little curve in his nose seemed ready for transformation. When he turned his head quickly, his hair appeared to scatter light. Some people saw definite genius in that sparkle. Mr. Casaubon, by contrast, gave out no rays.

Dorothea watched her husband anxiously. Perhaps she noticed the contrast, but it merely joined the other causes deepening her new anxiety for him. This was the beginning of a compassionate tenderness nourished by his real circumstances rather than her own dreams. Yet Will’s presence gave her greater freedom. The equality of his youth was pleasant, and perhaps so was his willingness to be persuaded. She felt an immense need for someone to talk to. Never before had she met anyone who seemed so quick and flexible, so likely to understand everything.

Mr. Casaubon gravely hoped Will was spending his time in Rome usefully as well as pleasantly. He had thought Will intended to remain in southern Germany. But he invited him to dinner the following day, when they could talk more fully; just now he was rather tired. Ladislaw understood, accepted, and immediately took his leave.

Dorothea’s anxious eyes followed her husband as he sank wearily onto the end of a sofa, supported his head on one hand with his elbow resting beside him, and looked at the floor. Flushed a little, her eyes bright, she sat next to him and said:
“Forgive me for speaking so hastily this morning. I was wrong. I’m afraid I hurt you and made your day harder.”
“I am glad you recognize that, my dear,” said Mr. Casaubon. His voice was quiet and he bent his head slightly, but his eyes still looked uneasy as he regarded her.

“But you do forgive me?” Dorothea asked with a sudden sob. Needing some display of feeling, she was ready to exaggerate her fault. Wouldn’t love see returning repentance from far away, run to embrace it, and kiss it?

“My dear Dorothea, ‘who with repentance is not satisfied, is not of heaven nor earth.’ You surely do not consider me deserving of banishment under that severe sentence,” said Mr. Casaubon, making an effort both to speak strongly and to smile faintly.
Dorothea did not answer, but a tear that had risen with the sob insisted on falling.

“You are overwrought, my dear. I too feel some unpleasant effects from excessive mental disturbance,” said Mr. Casaubon. He had actually been thinking of telling her she should not have received young Ladislaw while he was absent. He held back partly because introducing a new complaint during her repentant confession would be ungracious, partly because speaking would agitate him further, and partly because pride prevented him from revealing his jealous disposition. His scholarly rivals had not exhausted it so completely that none remained for other directions. There is a kind of jealousy that needs very little fire. It is scarcely passion at all, but a blight bred in the cloudy, damp discouragement of anxious self-concern.
“I think we should dress now,” he added, consulting his watch. They both stood up. Neither ever again referred to what had happened that day.

Dorothea, however, remembered it to the end of her life with the vividness we give to turning points when a cherished expectation dies or a new motive is born. That day she began to see how wildly mistaken she had been in expecting Mr. Casaubon to answer her feelings. She also felt the first intimation that his life might contain a painful awareness creating a need as great as her own.

We are all born morally stupid, treating the world as an udder to nourish our supremely important selves. Dorothea had begun early to emerge from that stupidity. Yet it had been easier to imagine devoting herself to Mr. Casaubon and becoming strong and wise through his strength and wisdom than to understand that he possessed an equally central self, from which light and shadow must always fall differently. She had not yet grasped this with the clarity that turns reflection into feeling, an idea made as immediate to the senses as the solidity of objects.
